items.name: The 2026 vintage, picked from 10 August
items.teaser: The Jura's first secateurs went in on 10 August: 'never started that early', growers told France 3
items.story: The 2026 Jura harvest began on 10 August, a date the Société de viticulture du Jura called fairly historic, about three weeks ahead of normal. The first rows cut were mostly grapes for Crémant; Chardonnay followed in late August, Savagnin and the red varieties during September. Early does not mean plentiful: on the society's network of 21 monitored plots, 29 per cent showed losses above half the crop, and growers spoke of pressure on the whole trade. The press still calls the vintage promising. The Savagnin picked this year goes under its veil now and will not be Vin Jaune until 2033 at the earliest.
items.why: Ask a grower about yields plot by plot: in 2026 they swung hard between neighbours.

The Maison de Louis Pasteur in Arbois opens every afternoon, 14:00 to 18:00, but its listings disagree on whether the winter close comes after 1 or 30 November: call. The Maison des Cascades at the Hérisson falls ran from 4 April to 30 September; the trails stay open, the centre does not. The Baume-les-Messieurs caves are visited from April to September only. The salt sites carry on: the Grande Saline at Salins-les-Bains opens daily 10:00–12:00 and 14:00–17:30 in November and December, and the Saline royale at Arc-et-Senans daily 10:00–17:00 from November to March. items.name: Mont d'Or, back since 10 September
items.teaser: Made only from 15 August to 15 March, sold only from 10 September to 10 May: the spruce-boxed winter cheese
items.story: Mont d'Or is the one Jura-massif cheese with a calendar written into law. Its AOP rules allow it to be made only from 15 August to 15 March and sold to the public only from 10 September to 10 May, so the first boxes reached the shops on 10 September 2026, three weeks after the first makes. Each soft wheel is girdled with spruce bark and sold in its spruce box. About 9.58 million cheeses were sold in the 2025–26 season. In Lons, look for it under the arcades at the fromager and on the Thursday cheese stalls.
items.why: Buy one per two or three people and ask the cheesemonger which week it was made.

items.name: The Biou d'Arbois before UNESCO
items.teaser: France's nomination for the intangible-heritage list goes to UNESCO's committee in November or December 2026
items.story: Each first weekend of September Arbois's growers build the Biou, a giant bunch of grapes, and carry it to the church of Saint-Just as an offering. France has put the Biou forward as its nomination for UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity; the town and the Société de viticulture gathered residents' consents for the file in 2024. Local agendas say the intergovernmental committee examines it at its 21st session, in November or December 2026 in China. UNESCO's own page lists the nomination as not inscribed; no session date was confirmed on UNESCO's site. The 2026 Biou ran on 5 and 6 September.
items.why: Follow the result in December: a yes would make the 2027 Biou the first under UNESCO.

bougie.title: 1264 — Salt, shared milk and a cheese built to keep
bougie.desc: How the Jura's salt trade and its village dairies, the fruitières, made Comté a cheese large enough to store, carry and sell.
bougie.lede: Comté is a cheese of scarcity turned into surplus. A mountain farm with a few cows could not make a wheel big enough to last the winter, so from the 13th century villages pooled their milk in shared dairies, the fruitières. Salt from Salins-les-Bains, a few hours away, was the region's wealth; the cheese became its other export.
paras: The springs of Salins-les-Bains may have been worked from about 4300 BC, and from the 13th century the town ran two saltworks, the Grande Saunerie and the Puits-à-Muire. By the late Middle Ages they produced about 7,400 tonnes a year, salt that supplied Franche-Comté, Switzerland and part of the duchy of Burgundy. In 1674 the two works merged under the French crown. When the forests that fuelled the pans ran short, the brine was piped to Ledoux's Saline royale at Arc-et-Senans, from 1779 to 1895.

The first fruitière's date is disputed. The European Commission's Comté page gives one founded at Déservillers in the Doubs in 1253; Alain Mélo's study of the Franche-Comté fruitières starts its chronology in 1264; a regional agriculture office names Déservillers in 1267 and Poligny in 1284 as the oldest known. The logic is not disputed: a large pressed, cooked wheel takes far more milk than one farm gives in a day, so neighbours pooled theirs. Early on, members took turns making cheese at home.

A court recognised the appellation in 1952, under the name Gruyère de Comté, and a decree created the AOC Comté in 1958. The trade's interprofession, the CIGC, was set up by decree in 1963 at Poligny, and European protection as a PDO followed in 1996, though one source gives 1992. Sources count between about 140 and 150 fruitières today, and 2024 rules cap merged dairies at 7.5 million litres a year. In 2025 the trade sold a record 62,480 tonnes.

_corrections: First fruitière: the brief's '1264–1273, Déservillers/Levier' is not confirmed as stated. Found: 1253 at Déservillers (European Commission), 1264 as the start of Mélo's chronology (Revue de géographie alpine), 1267 Déservillers and 1284 Poligny (DRAAF Bourgogne-Franche-Comté). No source for 1273 or for Levier was found. All three dates are given as disputed.

Salt and Comté: no source found states that the fruitières salted Comté with Salins or Lons salt specifically. The paragraphs place the salt trade and the cheese side by side without claiming the link as documented fact.

Comté AOC: 1952 was a court recognition (as Gruyère de Comté), 1958 the AOC decree; one source calls 1952 the first AOC, which contradicts the others. PDO: 1996 per Produits laitiers; BASIC gives 1992.
Tonnage: the old guide's 61,000 t in 2024 is consistent with 2025's 62,480 t being a 2.3 per cent rise (info.fr citing L'Est Républicain); 2025 is the figure used.
Fruitières today: 'about 140' (Bureau Veritas) versus 150 (INAO, Oligae); both given.
Salins closing date: sources disagree (1962 versus 1939 for the end of salt-making at Salins); not used.
Old guide: '400 litres per wheel' and '95% Montbéliarde' not re-verified here and left to The Dish.

Toussaint holidays 17 Oct–2 Nov 2026 for all zones; 1 Nov is a Sunday, 11 Nov a Wednesday. Grande Saline Nov–Dec 2026 hours from Jura Tourisme; Saline royale Nov–Mar 10:00–17:00 from Routard and a ticket site (not dated 2026). Bœuf sur le Toit dates from JDS/Songkick/AllEvents, not the hall's site; Cœur de Pirate 20 Nov is single-source. No November programme found for the Théâtre de Lons (Scènes du Jura season 11 Sep 2026–30 Jun 2027, details not found), so no theatre card. No November food fair or wine salon found in Lons, Arbois or Poligny beyond the Verrière evening and the Maison du Comté dates. No Fête du Vin Jaune or November Foire du Comté found. Lons Christmas 2026 dates are from one unconfirmed listing (27 Nov–3 Jan); 2025 was 28 Nov–4 Jan with the market on 13–14 Dec. Saline royale Christmas market dates are from one announcement (15 Oct 2026). Biou UNESCO session date (Nov/Dec 2026, China) is from local agendas; not confirmed on UNESCO's site. Percée 2027: Arlay, 6–7 Feb 2027, confirmed by several outlets; the vintage to be opened was not stated in the results and is not given. The old guide's founder claim (Bernard Badoz, 1997) and '32,000+' are not re-verified; 33,000 is the organiser's figure via Vinabox. Events cut: Livres dans la Boucle (Besançon), La Rodia, the natural-wine pilgrimage card (no dates), the flowering card (folded into seasonal rows), the 'Foire de Comté, Poligny, autumn' (not found; Comté events in Poligny are in August). 'Pâques en vins' and 'Les Jurassiennes' not found; omitted. The Festival de Musique du Haut-Jura is in late May, so it sits in Winter and spring, not Summer. Musiques en Haut is single-source. The Saline royale maps_query ends ', Doubs, France' because Arc-et-Senans is in the Doubs, not the Jura.
